Without support – for a short time
In cohesive soil above the groundwater, a vertical soil face temporarily stands down to a depth of m₀. For occupational safety, however, it has to be shored even at small depths.
E.g. a soldier pile wall or a spaced pile wall: embedded below excavation level, held by the passive earth resistance. As a cantilever only to about 4–6 m.
Wall anchored at one level
The top of the wall is held back by a ground anchor – the fixed length works beyond the active slip surface.
Watertight wall down to the impermeable layer
We have reached below the groundwater: a sheet pile, diaphragm, jet grout or slurry wall is needed, keyed into the impermeable clay – otherwise the excavation fills with water.
Wall anchored at several levels
Two rows of anchors. The anchors, 15–25 m long, reach under the neighbouring plot – a legal issue, and they can run into utilities or basements.
Tubular struts or supporting slabs
If anchoring is not possible, or the movement of the neighbouring building is critical: the stiff support of steel tubular struts or top-down supporting slabs.

Supporting slabs (levels: ${levels.length})
The slabs support the wall as diaphragms with great stiffness; they are cast on the ground, without falsework.
Nailed wall – a soil mass acting like a gravity wall

The nails “stitch together” the soil mass: nail length ≈ 0,6–1,2·H (here ~${fmt((P.gran ? 1.0 : 0.8) * H, 1)} m), grid 0,5–1,5 m, lifts every 0,9–1,8 m, wall batter max. 1:8–1:10.${H > 14 ? ' Ekkora mélységnél a deformációk már jelentősek lehetnek.' : ''}

Dry excavation
The groundwater (−${fmt(gw, 1)} m) is below the excavation level, no watertightness is needed.
Non-watertight wall + dewatering
The ${W.t.toLowerCase()} is not watertight: it can only be used with groundwater lowering. The drawdown also lowers the surrounding groundwater level – the neighbouring building may settle.
Water in the excavation!

The ${W.t.toLowerCase()} is not watertight, and the groundwater (−${fmt(gw, 1)} m) is above the excavation level: the excavation fills with water. Choose a watertight wall (sheet piles, diaphragm wall, secant pile wall, jet grout wall) or dewatering.
Watertight wall keyed into the impermeable layer

The toe of the wall (−${fmt(toe, 1)} m) reaches below the impermeable layer (−${fmt(P.imper, 1)} m): only the enclosed water has to be pumped out.${S.wall === 'jet' || S.wall === 'zagy' ? ' (A jet- és a zagyfal „kvázi vízzáró”.)' : ''}
(The jet grout and slurry walls are “quasi-watertight”.)
The wall does not reach the impermeable layer

The impermeable layer is at −${fmt(P.imper, 1)} m, and the ${W.t.toLowerCase()} is here at most about ${W.max} m long: water flows in from below (risk of hydraulic heave). Solution: a deeper wall (diaphragm wall), dewatering or underwater concreting.
Dewatering switched on
The groundwater is now below the excavation level – pumping is unnecessary.
Cannot be used in soft, plastic clay
Soil nailing does not work in soft, plastic clay, organic soil, rubble fill or boulders: the soil face does not stand even between the lifts.
Granular soil, fill at the top
In sandy gravel it only works if the lift (0,9–1,8 m) stands for a short time; in the top 2,5 m of rubble fill, nailing cannot be used – another solution is needed there.
Works well in hard clay
In hard, stony clay drilled and grouted nails are used; the soil face stands well between the lifts.
The nails reach under the neighbouring plot
Nails ${fmt(Ln, 1)} m long, the neighbouring building is ${fmt(dist, 1)} m away – a permit is needed, and they can run into the basement or utilities.
On the street side: utilities
In urban areas the densely spaced nails can run into the utilities under public land.
Spaced pile wall in soft soil
Soft soil does not arch between the piles, it flows out – a closed (contiguous, secant) wall is needed.
Spaced pile wall in granular soil
In granular soil the soil runs out between the piles: a contiguous pile wall or face protection (steel mesh + shotcrete) is needed.
Spaced pile wall in hard clay
In very hard clay the soil arches across the 20–60 cm gaps between the piles – this is the most widespread in Hungary.
Soldier pile wall in soft soil
In soft soil the face does not stand until the lagging is installed, and the soil can flow out from behind the planks.
One of the most economical temporary supports for dry, not too deep excavations; for noise reasons the soldiers are now more often set in bores.
Sheet piles in hard clay
In hard, stony clay the piles are hard to drive – pre-drilling is needed.
The vibration of driving and vibrating can reach as far as 20–30 m – it has to be checked for the building ${fmt(dist, 1)} m away (quieter: pressing-in).
Slurry wall depth
The reinforced self-hardening slurry wall is typically optimal for temporary excavations at most 7–10 m deep.${dist < H ? ' Süllyedésre érzékeny szerkezet közelében kerülendő.' : ''}
To be avoided near settlement-sensitive structures.
The slurry wall needs soil with favourable trench stability – in soft soil the trench can collapse.
Typically for 1–2-level underground car parks and later extensions; the column diameter depends on the soil (60–120 cm).${H > 10 ? ' Ekkora mélységhez inkább résfal.' : ''}
For this depth a diaphragm wall is better.
A watertight, stiff wall to great depth (even over 40 m); it can also be the permanent basement wall.
Watertight, but only every second pile is reinforced; compared with a diaphragm wall, economical only in special cases.
Wall too long
The required wall length of ${fmt(toe, 1)} m exceeds the usual limit of the technology (~${W.max} m).
Anchor length: max. ${fmt(longest, 1)} m

Free length beyond the active slip surface (min. 4 m) + fixed length (4–9 m, here 6 m), at an inclination of 15–30°; anchors are at most 25–30 m long. After hardening (8–12 days) they are stressed to 80–90% of the design force.
The anchor runs into the neighbour’s basement!
The top anchor row passes at the depth of the neighbouring building’s basement – a different inclination, a deeper level or a tubular strut is needed.
Anchor under the neighbouring plot
The anchors (often 15–20 m long) reach under the neighbouring property: a legal issue (consent), and they can run into existing structures.
Under the street: utilities
On the other side the anchors reach under public land – utilities have to be coordinated.
Fixity in soft soil
The fixed length falls in soft clay: low shaft friction, uncertain resistance – it has to be taken deeper.
Tubular strut span: ${fmt(B, 0)} m

Typically elements of 4–25 m; ${s === 'ok' ? 'ez a fesztáv közbenső alátámasztás nélkül is áthidalható.' : '25–28 m felett közbenső alátámasztás (pl. előre elkészített cölöpre) kell.'}${B > 12 ? ' 10–15 m felett a hőtágulásból eredő tengelyerő is meghatározó.' : ''}
this span can be bridged without intermediate support.
above 25–28 m intermediate support (e.g. on a pile made in advance) is needed.
Above 10–15 m the axial force from thermal expansion also governs.
Cramped working space
The struts hinder excavation and the construction of the internal structure – in return they do not reach under the neighbouring plot, and they give a stiff wall with small movements.
Top-down with a soldier pile wall?
The Milan method needs a retaining structure of a permanent nature that can carry the slabs (diaphragm wall, pile wall).
An unusual combination
For the top-down method a diaphragm wall or a pile wall is typically built – a ${WALLS[S.wall].t.toLowerCase()} is rarely used.
Roof slab, cramped working space
The surface can be handed back quickly; the excavation proceeds under the slab, through the muck-out opening, in a confined space – ventilation and lighting are needed.
